turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist here. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi, Dr. [Name]. I guess I'm here because... well, things at work have been really intense lately. I'm a buyer, you know, retail stuff, mostly electronics right now. Actually, I was just looking at this huge order of those new noise-canceling headphones, the ones with the really slick matte finish? They're supposed to be huge this quarter, but the shipping delays from overseas are just a nightmare. I was on the phone for two hours yesterday with this guy from logistics who sounded like he was eating a sandwich the whole time. 

But anyway, what really made me come in is... I just can't shake this feeling that people at work, and even some of the vendors, are tracking my buys. Like, they're messing with the launch numbers on purpose just to make me look stupid. My supervisor keeps pulling up these reports and trying to show me that the numbers don't prove it, but I know what I'm seeing. It's like they're all in on it. Which reminds me, my supervisor has this weird habit of tapping his pen when he's nervous, it drives me absolutely crazy. I tried to buy him a stress ball once, but he just left it on his desk gathering dust.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that coworkers and vendors are conspiring to sabotage their work, maintaining this conviction even when their supervisor presents contradictory evidence.

Actually, speaking of sneakers, did you know how complicated the secondary market is getting? There are these kids, like literally high schoolers, who write bots to buy up all the limited edition drops before regular people can even load the webpage. It's wild. I tried to set up a bot once, just to see how it works, and I ended up going down this massive rabbit hole about server proxies. You have to rent server space in the same zip code as the retailer's servers just to shave milliseconds off your ping time. Milliseconds! It's like high-frequency trading on Wall Street, but for shoes. And the crazy part is, my cousin in Chicago—he works at this deep-dish pizza place, terrible pizza honestly, way too much sauce—he actually bought a pair of those chunky dad shoes from one of those resellers for like eight hundred dollars. Eight hundred! For shoes that look like something a gym teacher wore in 1996. 

But yeah, anyway... I just feel like I'm operating on a completely different level than everyone else at work. Like I'm the one who's really running the show.
